why_how.text: Wheel position on a hill decides where a rolling car would go, so the handbook sets a rule for each case.
With no curb, turning the wheels right means a rolling car would leave the highway instead of entering traffic.

scenario.text: Sam parks facing uphill beside a curb on a steep street.

reasoning.text: Facing uphill at a curb, the front wheels point away from the curb and the car eases back until the curb blocks the front tire.

result.text: Sam turns the wheels away from the curb and lets the car ease back until the tire rests on the curb.

claim.text: Common mistake: turning the wheels toward the curb in every hill parking situation.

correction.text: Downhill means toward the curb, uphill means away from it, and with no curb the wheels go right either way.

prompt.text: You park facing downhill beside a curb. Which way should your front wheels point?

answer.text: Toward the curb, with the front tire resting against it.

rationale.text: Downhill at a curb means wheels toward it; uphill means away; no curb means right either way.

narration.text: This chapter opens with where your car sits when it is parked, then moves onto freeways, lane changes and passing. We start at the curb. You will learn how close to the curb to park where parallel parking is allowed, and how to turn your front wheels when you park on a hill. There are three hill cases: facing downhill beside a curb, facing uphill beside a curb, and parking on a hill where there is no curb at all. Each case has its own wheel position, and practice questions like to swap them, so we will keep each one tied to its own picture.

lines.text: Within twelve inches of the curb.
Or near the shoulder's outer edge.
So traffic is not blocked or slowed.

narration.text: Where parallel parking is allowed, park within twelve inches of the curb. If there is no curb, park as near as possible to the outer edge of the shoulder. The reason is stated right in the rule: so traffic is not blocked or slowed. A car parked far out from the curb narrows the lane for everyone passing by. When you finish parking, look at the gap between your tires and the curb. If it is more than twelve inches, adjust before you turn off the engine. That small step keeps the lane beside you clear for the traffic that is still moving.

lines.text: Uphill: wheels away from the curb.
Let the tire meet the curb.

narration.text: Parked facing downhill beside a curb, turn the front wheels toward the curb and let the car roll gently until the front tire rests against it. Parked facing uphill beside a curb, point the front wheels away from the curb and ease backward until the rear of the front tire is blocked by the curb. In both cases the curb ends up holding the front tire. The difference is which way the wheels point and which way the car settles. Downhill, the car rolls forward into the curb. Uphill, the car eases backward until the curb catches the back of the tire.

Here is the trap. Many learners remember only one hill rule and use it everywhere. With a curb, downhill means wheels toward the curb and uphill means wheels away from it. Without a curb, the wheels go right either way, whether you face uphill or downhill, so a rolling car would leave the highway instead of entering traffic. Questions mix these cases. One may describe an uphill spot with a curb and offer toward the curb. Another may describe a rural hill with no curb and offer turning left. Name the case first, then pick the matching wheel position.

lines.text: Which way do the wheels go?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you parallel park facing downhill on a street with a curb. Which way should your front wheels point, and what should the tire rest against? Decide before reading on. Turn the front wheels toward the curb and let the car roll gently until the front tire rests against it. If you were facing uphill, the wheels would point away from the curb and the car would ease back until the curb blocked the rear of the front tire. And on a hill with no curb, the wheels would go to the right in either direction.

Let us review. Where parallel parking is allowed, park within twelve inches of the curb, or as near as possible to the outer edge of the shoulder, so traffic is not blocked or slowed. Facing downhill beside a curb, turn the front wheels toward the curb until the front tire rests against it. Facing uphill beside a curb, point the wheels away and ease back until the curb blocks the rear of the front tire. With no curb, turn the wheels to the right either way, so a rolling car would leave the highway. Next, we move onto the freeway.

why_how.text: Freeways carry more traffic at higher speeds, so entering drivers must match speed and yield.
Ramp meters control how fast cars join, which is why a metered ramp is the one place you stop by design.

scenario.text: Lee drives onto an acceleration ramp beside busy freeway traffic.

reasoning.text: Build speed to match freeway traffic, and do not merge until the solid white line ends; freeway traffic has the right of way.

result.text: Lee speeds up to match traffic, waits for the solid line to end, finds a gap, and merges.

claim.text: Common mistake: stopping at the end of every entrance ramp before merging.

correction.text: Stopping in the acceleration lane is a last resort; the exception is a metered ramp, where you stop for the signal.

memory_support.text: Match speed; stop only at meters.

prompt.text: You reach a metered entrance ramp. When may you enter the freeway?

answer.text: After stopping at the signal and being released by a green light.

rationale.text: A ramp meter is the exception where you stop; on other ramps, stopping is a last resort.

narration.text: Freeways are built to carry more traffic at higher speeds than ordinary streets or highways. That is what makes them useful, and it is also what makes them dangerous. This lesson covers how to join a freeway safely. You will learn what to do on an acceleration ramp, how to enter from a side entrance ramp, when you may merge across from the acceleration lane, who has the right of way, and what to do at a metered ramp with a signal. One idea runs through all of it: you fit into freeway traffic, and freeway traffic does not stop for you.

Freeways are dangerous because of the high speeds involved, so stay aware of everything around you at all times. At freeway speeds, the gap between a safe move and a crash closes quickly. A driver who drifts, merges without looking, or misses a slowdown ahead has very little time to recover. Staying aware means knowing what is ahead, what is beside you and what is behind you, not just the car directly in front. Keep that full awareness from the moment you start up the ramp until you have left the freeway and slowed to the speed of the road you join.

lines.text: Side entrance: signal, gap, speed, merge.

narration.text: On an acceleration ramp, build up speed to match freeway traffic before you merge. Entering at a speed far below traffic forces freeway drivers to brake or swerve. To enter from a side entrance ramp, signal, look for a gap, speed up to the traffic speed and merge only when it is safe. The order matters: signal so others know your plan, find the gap you will use, match the speed of the traffic around that gap, and then move in. If no safe gap appears, keep looking rather than forcing your way in. A smooth merge depends on matching speed.

lines.text: Do not merge until it ends.
Avoid stopping in the acceleration lane.
Freeway traffic has the right of way.

narration.text: Do not merge until the solid white line ends. The solid line separates the ramp from the freeway, and crossing it early cuts into traffic where drivers do not expect you. Avoid stopping in the acceleration lane unless it is truly necessary, because a stopped car on a ramp has to rejoin fast traffic from a standstill. And remember that freeway traffic has the right of way. Drivers already on the freeway are not required to make room for you, although many will. Your job is to match their speed and slip into a gap without forcing anyone to brake.

lines.text: At a ramp meter: stop for the signal.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers stop at the end of every entrance ramp to look before merging, while others roll through a ramp meter without stopping. Both are wrong. When entering a freeway, you match its speed and yield to it, and stopping in the acceleration lane is a last resort. The exception is a metered ramp, where you stop for the signal. So the meter is the one place where stopping on a ramp is the plan, not a fallback. Everywhere else, keep moving, build speed, and find a gap. Questions test whether you can tell the two kinds of ramp apart.

Here is a quick check: you are driving up an entrance ramp and see a signal near the end of the ramp, turned red. What should you do, and when may you enter the freeway? Decide before reading on. This is a metered entrance ramp. Stop at the signal and enter the freeway only when released by a green light. On an ordinary ramp with no meter, you would instead build speed to match traffic, wait until the solid white line ends, and merge into a safe gap, stopping only as a last resort. In both cases, freeway traffic has the right of way.

lines.text: Stop only at a ramp meter.

narration.text: Let us review. Freeways are built to carry more traffic at higher speeds, and the high speeds make them dangerous, so stay aware at all times. On an acceleration ramp, build up speed to match freeway traffic before you merge. From a side entrance ramp, signal, look for a gap, speed up to traffic speed and merge only when safe. Do not merge until the solid white line ends, avoid stopping in the acceleration lane unless truly necessary, and remember freeway traffic has the right of way. On a metered ramp, stop at the signal and go on green. Next, freeway lanes.

why_how.text: Lane roles keep slower drivers out of the way of passing traffic.
Making room at merges and scanning all around keep freeway traffic flowing safely.

scenario.text: Mia is driving slower than traffic in the leftmost freeway lane, with no plan to pass.

reasoning.text: The rightmost lane is for slower drivers, and the leftmost lane is for passing, left turns and heavy traffic.

result.text: Mia signals at least two hundred feet ahead and moves to the rightmost lane.

claim.text: Common mistake: cruising in the leftmost lane while going slower than other traffic.

correction.text: The leftmost lane is for passing, left turns and heavy-traffic situations; slower drivers use the rightmost lane.

prompt.text: You are driving slower than normal freeway traffic. Which lane should you be in?

rationale.text: The rightmost lane is for slower drivers, while the leftmost lane is for passing and the listed uses.

narration.text: Once you are on the freeway, a new set of rules takes over. This lesson covers which lane to use depending on your speed, what the leftmost lane is for, how to help drivers who are entering at a merge, what you should be watching while you drive, and the special rules for changing lanes on a freeway. These rules are about cooperation. When every driver uses the lanes for their intended purpose and makes room for others, traffic flows, and the high speeds of the freeway stay manageable. When drivers ignore them, the freeway gets crowded and risky quickly.

lines.text: Or heavy traffic with no room to merge.

narration.text: Use the rightmost lane when you are going slower than normal traffic speed. The leftmost lane is the passing lane. It is for passing, for left turns, and for times when heavy traffic leaves no room to merge into the other lanes. So a driver who is not passing, not turning left, and not boxed in by heavy traffic should not be cruising in the leftmost lane. Keeping slower vehicles to the right leaves the left lane open for those who need to pass, which cuts down on drivers weaving between lanes to get around someone who is blocking.

Here is the trap. Many drivers settle into the leftmost lane and stay there at whatever speed they like. The rightmost freeway lane is for slower drivers, while the leftmost lane is reserved for passing, left turns and heavy-traffic situations. Questions may describe a driver going slower than traffic in the left lane and ask whether that is the right lane choice. It is not. Others may ask what the leftmost lane is for and offer slow driving as an answer. Match the lane to its job: slower traffic to the right, passing to the left.

lines.text: Near a merge, move over when safe.
Know your blind spots; read guide signs.

narration.text: Approaching a merge area, move over when it is safe to give entering vehicles room. You are not required to, but moving over helps entering drivers join smoothly. On the freeway, watch traffic ahead, beside and behind you, and stay aware of vehicles in your blind spots. Plan ahead with directional and guide signs, so you know which lane you will need for your exit well before you reach it. Planning ahead is what lets you make one calm lane change instead of a sudden dash across several lanes at the last moment. Keep right unless passing.

lines.text: Signal at least two hundred feet ahead.
Never cross a median or island.

narration.text: On the freeway, signal at least two hundred feet before a lane change, avoid changing lanes often, and never drive across, over or inside a median or island. Frequent lane changes add risk with every move, so pick a lane that suits your speed and stay in it as much as you can. The median rule matters most when a driver realizes they have missed an exit or need to turn around. Crossing a median or island is never the answer. Instead, continue to the next exit. The full routine for any lane change comes in the lesson after next.

Here is a quick check: you are on a three-lane freeway, driving a bit slower than the traffic around you, and you are not planning to pass or turn left. Which lane should you be in, and how do you get there? Decide before reading on. Use the rightmost lane, because it is for drivers going slower than normal traffic. The leftmost lane is for passing, left turns and heavy-traffic situations. To move over, signal at least two hundred feet before the lane change, then move when it is safe, and try not to change lanes more often than you need to.

lines.text: Signal early; never cross a median.

narration.text: Let us review. Use the rightmost lane when you are going slower than normal traffic. The leftmost lane is for passing, left turns, and heavy traffic that leaves no room to merge elsewhere. Approaching a merge area, move over when safe to give entering vehicles room. Watch traffic ahead, beside and behind you, stay aware of your blind spots, and plan with guide signs. On the freeway, signal at least two hundred feet before a lane change, avoid changing lanes often, and never drive across, over or inside a median or island. Next, leaving the freeway.

why_how.text: Slowing in the deceleration lane keeps your speed change out of the path of freeway traffic.
Last-second exits force sudden moves across lanes, so the handbook says to plan the exit.

scenario.text: Ana sees her exit ahead, with a deceleration lane beginning before the ramp.

reasoning.text: Signal two hundred feet before the deceleration lane begins, hold speed until in it, then slow to the advised ramp speed.

result.text: Ana signals early, keeps pace into the deceleration lane, then slows there to the posted ramp speed.

claim.text: Common mistake: braking on the freeway itself before reaching the exit lane.

correction.text: Keep your speed until you are inside the deceleration lane, and slow down there, not on the freeway.

memory_support.text: Hold speed, then slow in the lane.

prompt.text: Where should you slow down when you exit a freeway?

rationale.text: You hold your speed until you are in the deceleration lane, then slow to the advised exit ramp speed.

narration.text: Getting off a freeway safely takes as much planning as getting on. This lesson covers the deceleration lane, when to signal for your exit, where to slow down, and the habits that keep exits calm: keeping pace with traffic, never exiting at the last second, and respecting the posted ramp limit. The most common error is slowing down too early, while still in a freeway travel lane, which surprises the drivers behind you. The handbook places the slowdown in a specific spot, and learning that spot is the main goal of this short lesson.

lines.text: Signal two hundred feet before it begins.
Hold your speed until you are in it.
Then slow to the advised ramp speed.

narration.text: To exit, use the deceleration lane. Signal two hundred feet before the deceleration lane begins, so drivers behind you know your plan. Hold your speed until you are in the deceleration lane, then slow to the advised exit ramp speed. The deceleration lane exists to give you a place to slow down away from the faster freeway traffic. If you brake while still in a freeway travel lane, you force the drivers behind you to brake too. By moving over first and slowing second, you keep the speed change out of their path. Move over first, slow second.

title.text: Slow in the lane, not before

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers start braking on the freeway itself as soon as they see their exit sign. On the exit, you keep your speed until you are inside the deceleration lane and slow down there, not on the freeway itself. A practice question may describe a driver who brakes in the right travel lane before the exit and ask whether that is correct. It is not. The correct order is signal, move into the deceleration lane at freeway speed, and then slow. The deceleration lane is named for exactly that job, so let it do the work.

lines.text: Keep pace with traffic until the exit.
Do not exit at the last second.
Do not exceed the posted ramp limit.

narration.text: When leaving a freeway, keep pace with traffic until the exit, do not exit at the last second, and do not exceed the posted ramp limit. Keeping pace means not slowing early in a travel lane. Not exiting at the last second means planning ahead with guide signs, so you are in the correct lane well before the exit and do not have to cut across lanes. And the ramp limit matters because exit ramps often curve and lead to slower roads. If you do miss your exit, the earlier lesson applies: never cross a median or island; continue to the next exit.

Here is a quick check: your exit is coming up, and you have signaled and checked your mirrors. Where should you slow down, and to what speed? Think it through before reading on. Hold your speed until you are inside the deceleration lane, then slow there to the advised exit ramp speed. Do not slow down on the freeway itself. Remember to signal two hundred feet before the deceleration lane begins, keep pace with traffic until the exit, never exit at the last second, and do not exceed the posted ramp limit once you are on the ramp.

lines.text: Plan ahead; obey the ramp limit.

narration.text: Let us review. To exit a freeway, use the deceleration lane. Signal two hundred feet before it begins, hold your speed until you are in it, then slow to the advised exit ramp speed. Slow down inside the deceleration lane, not on the freeway itself. When leaving, keep pace with traffic until the exit, do not exit at the last second, and do not exceed the posted ramp limit. Planning your exit early with guide signs is what makes each of these steps easy. Next, we look closely at the full routine for changing lanes. Plan your exit early.

why_how.text: Every lane change crosses someone's path, so each one requires checking ahead, beside and behind.
The blind spot is invisible in mirrors, which is why the shoulder look is part of the routine.

scenario.text: Kai wants to move into the left lane on a busy road.

reasoning.text: Signal for at least three seconds or two hundred feet, check ahead, check mirrors, look over the shoulder, then move when safe.

result.text: Kai spots a car in the blind spot on the shoulder look, waits for it to pass, then moves over and cancels the signal.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a mirror check alone is enough before changing lanes.

correction.text: Mirrors are not enough, because the blind spot just behind and beside you needs an over-the-shoulder look.

prompt.text: Why must you look over your shoulder before changing lanes, even with good mirrors?

answer.text: Because the blind spot is an area neither the rearview nor side mirrors show.

rationale.text: Mirrors are not enough for a lane change; the blind spot needs an over-the-shoulder look.

lines.text: What counts as a lane change.

narration.text: Changing lanes is something you will do thousands of times, and the handbook lays out a full routine for it. This lesson starts with what counts as a lane change, which covers more moves than many people think. Then it defines the blind spot, explains why mirrors alone cannot cover it, walks through the step-by-step routine, and finishes with what to do after the move, including when to switch off your signal. If you build the routine into a habit now, it will run automatically, even in heavy traffic when you have a lot on your mind.

lines.text: Pulling out from a curb or shoulder.

narration.text: A lane change includes moving between lanes, passing, merging from an entrance ramp, and pulling onto the road from a curb or shoulder. Each of these requires checking ahead, beside and behind. That list is broader than many drivers assume. Pulling away from a parking spot at the curb is a lane change in this sense, and so is merging from an on-ramp. In every case, you are moving into a space that someone else might be using or about to use. So the same careful checks apply to all of them, not just to switching lanes on a highway.

lines.text: Slightly to the side and rear.
Not shown by rearview or side mirrors.

narration.text: A blind spot is an area slightly to the side and rear of your vehicle that neither the rearview mirror nor the side mirrors show. A car, a motorcycle or a bicyclist can sit in that area without appearing in any mirror. That is why a driver can check every mirror, see nothing, start to move over, and still hit someone. The only way to see into your blind spot is to turn your head and look over your shoulder. The look is quick, just long enough to confirm the space beside you is empty, and then your eyes return to the road ahead.

lines.text: Look over your shoulder every time.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers believe that well-adjusted mirrors make the shoulder look unnecessary. Mirrors are not enough for a lane change, because the blind spot just behind and beside you needs an over-the-shoulder look. Practice questions may describe a driver who signals, checks both mirrors, sees nothing, and moves over, then ask what they missed. The answer is the look over the shoulder into the blind spot. Treat that look as a required step in every lane change, merge, pass, and pull-out from a curb or shoulder, not an optional extra.

lines.text: Signal: three seconds or two hundred feet.
Look over your shoulder; move when safe.

narration.text: To change lanes, signal for at least three seconds or two hundred feet. Check ahead. Check the mirrors. Look over your shoulder at the blind spot. Then move over when it is safe. Once you are centered in the new lane, glance at the mirror for traffic behind you, and switch the signal off no more than three seconds after the change is complete. Each step has a job. The signal warns others, the check ahead makes sure the lane you want is clear in front, the mirrors show the lane behind, and the shoulder look covers what the mirrors miss.

lines.text: Why still look over your shoulder?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: your mirrors are set correctly, and when you check them before a lane change, the next lane looks empty. Why should you still look over your shoulder before moving over? Decide before reading on. Because a blind spot is an area slightly to the side and rear of your vehicle that neither the rearview nor side mirrors show. Mirrors are not enough for a lane change. Signal for at least three seconds or two hundred feet, check ahead, check mirrors, look over your shoulder, move when safe, then cancel the signal within three seconds.

Let us review. A lane change includes moving between lanes, passing, merging from an entrance ramp and pulling onto the road from a curb or shoulder, and each requires checking ahead, beside and behind. A blind spot is an area slightly to the side and rear that no mirror shows, so mirrors are not enough. Signal for at least three seconds or two hundred feet, check ahead, check the mirrors, look over your shoulder, then move over when safe. Once centered, glance at the mirror and switch the signal off within three seconds. Next, passing.

why_how.text: Passing puts you in another lane at higher speed, so signs and markings show where it is allowed.
Passing one vehicle at a time keeps the time you spend in another lane short.

scenario.text: On a two-lane road, Jo is stuck behind a slow car and sees a wide paved shoulder on the right.

reasoning.text: Passing on the right is allowed only on one-way streets and roads with two or more lanes each way, and never on the shoulder.

result.text: Jo stays behind the car until it is safe and legal to pass on the left.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a wide shoulder makes passing on the right acceptable.

correction.text: Passing on the right is allowed on one-way streets and roads with two or more lanes each way, but passing on the shoulder or off the pavement never is.

prompt.text: You are on a road with two or more lanes each way. Is passing on the right allowed?

rationale.text: Passing on the right is allowed on one-way streets and roads with two or more lanes each way, but never on the shoulder.

lines.text: Time, room and one at a time.

narration.text: Passing is one of the riskier moves in driving, because it puts you in another lane, often at a higher speed, for longer than an ordinary lane change. This lesson is about the decision to pass: where passing is allowed, which side you pass on, the narrow cases where passing on the right is legal, what you must judge before you start, and why you pass only one vehicle at a time. The next lesson covers how to finish a pass safely. Together they cover the whole move, from deciding whether to pass to returning to your own lane.

lines.text: Passing is normally on the left.

narration.text: Signs and markings show where passing is and is not allowed, and passing is normally done on the left. You already learned the yellow line rules in an earlier chapter. A broken yellow line on your side allows passing when safe, and a solid line on your side does not. Signs can add to this, for example by marking a no-passing zone. The basic picture is simple: on most roads you pass by moving into the lane to your left, overtaking, and returning to the right. Exceptions to that picture are few, and the next slide covers them.

lines.text: Roads with two or more lanes each way.
Never on the shoulder or off the pavement.

narration.text: Passing on the right is allowed only on one-way streets and on roads with two or more lanes each way. Passing by driving off the pavement or on the shoulder is never allowed. So on an ordinary two-lane road with one lane each way, there is no legal pass on the right, even if the car ahead is waiting to turn left and the shoulder looks wide. On a multi-lane road, passing on the right can happen naturally when the left lane is moving more slowly. In every case, the pass happens in a travel lane, never on the shoulder or the dirt beside the road.

lines.text: Right-side passing: only in the listed cases.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A wide, paved shoulder can look like an invitation to pass. Passing on the right is allowed on one-way streets and roads with two or more lanes each way, but passing on the shoulder or off the pavement never is. Questions may describe a two-lane road with a stopped car waiting to turn left and offer passing on the shoulder as an answer. It is not allowed. Others may describe a one-way street and ask whether passing on the right is legal. It is. The deciding question is whether the pass stays in a travel lane on a road where right-side passing is allowed.

lines.text: Enough time and room, bicyclists included.
Pass one vehicle at a time.

narration.text: Before passing anyone, bicyclists included, judge from traffic ahead, beside and behind whether you have enough time and room to do it safely. That means looking down the road for oncoming traffic, checking beside you for anyone in the lane you will use, and checking behind for anyone already starting to pass you. Pass only one vehicle at a time rather than counting on passing several at once. Trying to pass a line of cars keeps you in the other lane much longer, and leaves you with nowhere to go if the gap you were counting on disappears.

lines.text: Two or more lanes each way.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are on a road with two or more lanes in each direction, and the car in the left lane ahead is moving slowly. Is passing on the right allowed here? And would it change anything if you used the shoulder instead? Decide before reading on. Passing on the right is allowed on roads with two or more lanes each way and on one-way streets. Passing by driving on the shoulder or off the pavement is never allowed. Before any pass, judge whether you have enough time and room, and pass only one vehicle at a time.

Let us review. Signs and markings show where passing is and is not allowed, and passing is normally done on the left. Passing on the right is allowed only on one-way streets and roads with two or more lanes each way, and passing off the pavement or on the shoulder is never allowed. Before passing anyone, bicyclists included, judge from traffic ahead, beside and behind whether you have enough time and room. Pass only one vehicle at a time. Next, we look at how to finish a pass and return to your lane safely. Stay in a travel lane.

why_how.text: Returning only when both headlights show in your mirror leaves the passed driver safe space.
The distance from oncoming traffic and the solid yellow line both mark when a pass must already be finished.

scenario.text: Eli is passing a slow truck on a two-lane road when he sees a solid yellow line beginning ahead.

reasoning.text: Do not pass if you cannot get back to the right side before a solid yellow line begins.

result.text: Eli sees he cannot finish in time, so he eases back behind the truck before the solid line begins.

claim.text: Common mistake: cutting back in as soon as your front bumper clears the passed vehicle.

correction.text: Return to your lane once both headlights of the passed vehicle appear in your rearview mirror.

prompt.text: You are passing a car. When should you return to your lane?

answer.text: When both of its headlights appear in your rearview mirror.

rationale.text: A finished pass means both headlights in your mirror and back before any solid yellow line begins.

narration.text: Starting a pass is only half the job. This lesson covers how to pass properly and, most importantly, when you must already be back in your own lane. You will learn the headlight rule for returning, the distance you must keep from oncoming vehicles, and why a solid yellow line ahead can mean you should not start a pass at all. Each of these rules is about the end of the pass, but you apply them before you begin. If you cannot meet them, the right decision is to wait for a better place to pass rather than starting and hoping it works out.

To pass, change lanes properly, using the full lane-change routine from the earlier lesson. Speed up past the vehicle. Return to your lane once both of its headlights appear in your rearview mirror. Seeing both headlights tells you there is enough room between your car and the one you passed, so you will not cut it off when you move back. If you return too soon, the driver you passed may have to brake hard. So keep going until the headlight check is met, then signal, check, and move back into your own lane. Then move back smoothly.

lines.text: More than two hundred feet from oncoming.

narration.text: Never start a pass unless you can be back on the right side while still more than two hundred feet from any oncoming vehicle. That includes a bicyclist in the oncoming lane or on the oncoming shoulder. The rule is about planning. Before you pull out, look ahead and judge whether you will be back in your lane with that much space to spare. If an oncoming vehicle is close enough that you might not make it, do not start. A bicyclist on the far shoulder is easy to overlook, so look for riders as well as cars before committing to the pass.

lines.text: Back before a solid yellow line.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Learners often remember one finishing rule and forget the other. Return to your lane after passing when you see both headlights of the passed vehicle in the rearview mirror, and finish before a solid yellow line begins. Do not pass if you cannot get back to the right side before a solid yellow line begins. A practice question may describe a driver who meets the headlight rule but crosses back after the solid line has started, or one who cuts back early to reach the line first. Both are wrong. A proper pass meets both conditions, plus the oncoming distance.

Here is a quick check: you are partway through passing a car on a two-lane road. Your front bumper has just cleared its front bumper. Should you move back now? Decide before reading on. Not yet. Return to your lane once both of the passed vehicle's headlights appear in your rearview mirror. And the pass must be finished before a solid yellow line begins, while you are still more than two hundred feet from any oncoming vehicle. If you cannot meet those conditions, you should not have started the pass, so ease back and wait.

lines.text: Over two hundred feet from oncoming.

narration.text: Let us review. To pass, change lanes properly, speed up past the vehicle, and return to your lane once both of its headlights appear in your rearview mirror. Never start a pass unless you can be back on the right side while still more than two hundred feet from any oncoming vehicle, counting a bicyclist in the oncoming lane or shoulder. Do not pass if you cannot get back to the right side before a solid yellow line begins. Plan the end of the pass before you start it. Next, we finish the chapter with passing bicyclists.

why_how.text: A bicyclist has no protection, so the clearance is measured to the widest part of your vehicle.
Wind from a large or fast vehicle can knock a rider over, which is why some situations call for extra room.

scenario.text: Ben, towing a trailer, comes up behind a bicyclist on a rural road with a solid yellow line and no oncoming traffic.

reasoning.text: Leave at least three feet to the outermost part, including the trailer; you may briefly cross the solid yellow line with no oncoming traffic and a clear view.

result.text: Ben gives the rider extra room, crosses the yellow line briefly with a clear view, and returns once safely past.

claim.text: Common mistake: measuring the three feet from the side of the car body and ignoring mirrors or a trailer.

correction.text: The three feet run between the rider and the outermost part of your vehicle, including mirrors or a trailer.

memory_support.text: Three feet from the widest part.

prompt.text: When passing a bicyclist, what part of your vehicle do you measure the three feet from?

answer.text: The outermost part, including mirrors or a trailer.

rationale.text: The clearance runs to the outermost part of the vehicle, and extra room is wise on rural roads, in a large vehicle or in wind.

narration.text: Bicyclists share many roads with cars, and passing them safely takes a few specific rules. This lesson covers the minimum clearance and how it is measured, the one situation where you may briefly cross a solid yellow line to pass a rider, and the conditions that call for even more room than the minimum. You have met the three-foot rule before; here you will see the detail that is easy to miss, which is where the three feet are measured from. These rules work together with the passing rules from the last two lessons, including judging time and room.

title.text: Three feet to the widest part

lines.text: At least three feet of clearance.
To the outermost part of your vehicle.

narration.text: When passing a bicyclist, keep at least three feet between the rider and the outermost part of your vehicle, including mirrors or a trailer. So the three feet are not measured from the side of your car door. They are measured from whatever sticks out farthest, which may be a side mirror, a wide load, or a trailer behind you. A driver who leaves three feet from the car body may pass much closer than that with a mirror. Before you pass, picture the widest part of your vehicle and make sure the full three feet separate it from the rider.

lines.text: Briefly cross a solid yellow line.
Only with a clear view ahead.

narration.text: To pass a bicyclist, you may briefly cross a solid yellow line when no traffic is oncoming and your view ahead is clear. This exception exists so that drivers can give riders the required room on narrow roads. Both conditions must be met. If a car is coming, or if a curve or hill blocks your view of the road ahead, you must wait behind the rider. And the crossing is brief: move over just enough to give the clearance, pass, and return to your lane. This is not permission to pass cars across a solid yellow line, only bicyclists.

Here is the trap. Many drivers think they gave a rider three feet because the side of the car was three feet away. The handbook measures the three feet between the rider and the outermost part of your vehicle, including mirrors or a trailer. Questions may describe a driver towing a trailer who leaves three feet from the car but less from the trailer, and ask whether the rule was met. It was not. The clearance belongs to the widest point. Give bicyclists extra room on rural roads, in a large vehicle or in wind, because a wind blast can knock a rider over.

Here is a quick check: you are driving a pickup with wide side mirrors and towing a small trailer, and you need to pass a bicyclist. From what part of your vehicle should the three feet of clearance be measured? Decide before reading on. From the outermost part of your vehicle, including the mirrors or the trailer, whichever sticks out farthest. Because you are in a larger vehicle, give the rider extra room as well, since a wind blast can knock a rider over. If a solid yellow line is beside you, cross it only briefly, with no oncoming traffic and a clear view.

lines.text: Three feet to the widest part.

narration.text: Let us close the chapter. When passing a bicyclist, keep at least three feet between the rider and the outermost part of your vehicle, including mirrors or a trailer. To pass a bicyclist, you may briefly cross a solid yellow line when no traffic is oncoming and your view ahead is clear. Give bicyclists extra room on rural roads, in a large vehicle or in wind, because a wind blast can knock a rider over. Combined with the passing rules, these keep riders safe.
